name: Thangmi
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Turin, Mark. 2012. A Grammar of the Thangmi Language. Brill (paywalled; phonology chapter plausibly covers stress)

new_statements.quote: In Thangmi, stress is non-distinctive, prosodic and relatively unpronounced. In glossary entries in the lexicon, stress is indicated by a stress mark [ " ] before the stressed syllable, but only in instances when it is not predictable. Unless otherwise indicated, all Thangmi words are stressed on the first syllable. The only deviations from this rule relate to Thangmi verb forms composed of three syllables of more, in which the stress falls on the second syllable: [...] Reflexive verbs follow a slightly different pattern with regard to word and syllable stress. Since the reflexive marker <-si> (REF) is never stressed, the stress always falls on the preceding syllable [...] Inflected verb forms do not deviate from the above rules
new_statements.citation: Turin, Mark. 2004. The phonology of Thangmi: a Tibeto-Burman language of Nepal. Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA, Tokyo) 67: 63-103.
new_statements.locator: Section 4.1 'Stress', pp. 94-95 (the same rule is restated in the abstract, p. 63; and verbatim in Turin 2019, Gipan 4, p. 65)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive and is weakly realised. Default: first syllable of the word (nouns, adjectives, one- and two-syllable verbs, e.g. ['hara] 'what?', ['akjarak] 'arum bulb', ['bosa] 'to grow'). Exception: verb forms (stems and inflected forms) of three or more syllables carry stress on the second syllable (e.g. [kE'rEpsa] 'to cry', [tsi'nampasa] 'to cause to play', [kE'rEpNan] 'I cried'). The reflexive suffix -si is never stressed, so in reflexive verbs stress stays on the syllable preceding -si (e.g. ['phaksisa], [thaNNa'raNsisa]). Unpredictable cases are marked in the lexicon.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb forms of three or more syllables (second-syllable stress); reflexive verbs (stress on the syllable before -si); lexical entries with unpredictable stress are marked with a stress mark in the glossary; Nepali loans may deviate from the canonical syllable scheme (fn. 7).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (citation forms and inflected verb forms); a separate phrase/sentence-level prosodic accent is realised as vowel lengthening (section 5, p. 101). The article describes the Dolakha dialect of Thangmi.
new_statements.identity_note: Turin 2004 explicitly describes the phonology of the Dolakha dialect of Thangmi (Glottolog than1259 covers the language as a whole; Turin notes two mutually unintelligible dialects, Dolakha and Sindhupalcok). The name Thami (Nepali) is the same language.

sources.locator: Section 4.1 'Stress', pp. 94-95 (the same rule is restated in the abstract, p. 63; and verbatim in Turin 2019, Gipan 4, p. 65)
sources.note: Section 4.1 'Stress' (pp. 94-95): stress is non-distinctive, prosodic and relatively unpronounced; all words stressed on the first syllable, except verb forms of three or more syllables, which stress the second syllable; reflexive -si is never stressed so stress falls on the preceding syllable; inflected verb forms follow the same rules. Section 5 adds that vowel lengthening marks the prosodic accent of a clause/sentence. Describes the Dolakha dialect.

sources.note: p. 65: 'Stress is non-distinctive, prosodic and relatively unpronounced in Thangmi. Unless otherwise indicated, all Thangmi words are stressed on the first syllable. The only deviations from this rule are Thangmi verb forms composed of three syllables of more, in which the stress falls on the second syllable.' Restates the 2004/2012 rule.
